section.title: The Snare of the Adulteress
section.sectionRationale: The theme begun in chapter 5 reaches its fullest and most dramatic treatment here. Parental instruction against the adulteress, 6:20 to 24, moves into the devastating cost of adultery, 6:25 to 35, then a fresh appeal to treasure wisdom as a close kinswoman, 7:1 to 5, before the discourse becomes a narrated scene, a father watching from his window as a naive young man is lured step by step to his own destruction, 7:6 to 27.
section.thesis: The adulteress promises pleasure but delivers fire, wounds, and a road to death, and the only sure guard against her is treasuring wisdom's instruction as intimately as one treasures family, since a heart without that guard will, like the watched young man, walk unknowingly into the slaughter.
section.frameNote: Five movements: parental instruction against the adulteress, 6:20 to 24; the devastating cost of adultery, 6:25 to 35; the appeal to keep wisdom as close as family, 7:1 to 5; the narrated scene of a young man's seduction, 7:6 to 23, the section's dramatic climax; and the closing warning that her house is the road to Sheol, 7:24 to 27.

verses.text: My son, keep your father's commandment, and do not forsake your mother's teaching.
Bind them always upon your heart; tie them around your neck.
When you walk, they will guide you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; when you awake, they will speak to you.
For this commandment is a lamp, this teaching is a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way to life,
to keep you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the {{nokriyah|adulteress}}.
Do not lust in your heart for her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes.
For the levy of the prostitute is poverty, and the adulteress preys upon your very life.
Can a man embrace fire and his clothes not be burned?
Can a man walk on hot coals without scorching his feet?
So is he who sleeps with another man's wife; no one who touches her will go unpunished.
Men do not despise the thief if he steals to satisfy his hunger.
Yet if caught, he must pay sevenfold; he must give up all the wealth of his house.
He who commits adultery lacks judgment; whoever does so destroys himself.
Wounds and dishonor will befall him, and his reproach will never be wiped away.
For {{qinah|jealousy}} enrages a husband, and he will show no mercy in the day of vengeance.
He will not be appeased by any ransom, or persuaded by lavish gifts.

units.label: Keep wisdom as close as family

verses.text: My son, keep my words and treasure my commandments within you.
Keep my commandments and live; guard my teachings as the apple of your eye.
Tie them to your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.
Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call understanding your kinsman,
that they may keep you from the adulteress, from the stranger with seductive words.

units.label: A young man watched and lured

verses.text: For at the window of my house I looked through the lattice.
I saw among the simple, I noticed among the youths, a {{peti|young man lacking judgment}},
crossing the street near her corner, strolling down the road to her house,
at twilight, as the day was fading into the dark of the night.
Then a woman came out to meet him, with the attire of a harlot and cunning of heart.
She is loud and defiant; her feet do not remain at home.
Now in the street, now in the squares, she lurks at every corner.
She seizes him and kisses him; she brazenly says to him:
"I have made my peace offerings; today I have paid my vows.
So I came out to meet you; I sought you, and I have found you.
I have decked my bed with coverings, with colored linen from Egypt.
I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, with aloes, and with cinnamon.
Come, let us take our fill of love till morning. Let us delight in loving caresses!
For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey.
He took with him a bag of money and will not return till the moon is full."
With her great persuasion she entices him; with her flattering lips she lures him.
He follows her on impulse, like an ox going to the slaughter, like a deer bounding into a trap,
until an arrow pierces his liver, like a bird darting into a snare, not knowing it will cost him his life.

units.label: Her house is the road to Sheol

verses.text: Now, my sons, listen to me, and attend to the words of my mouth.
Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths.
For she has brought many down to death; her slain are many in number.
Her house is the road to Sheol, descending to the chambers of death.

nokriyah.gloss: The foreign or adulterous woman, literally the one made a stranger through covenant unfaithfulness. Her smooth tongue, 6:24, and seductive words, 7:5, are named as the very dangers a father's teaching is meant to guard against.

qinah.gloss: Jealousy, here the righteous, unappeasable anger of a betrayed husband, 6:34. The word can describe both destructive envy and righteous zeal for what is rightfully one's own, and here it names the very real, human cost adultery inflicts on a marriage.

peti.gloss: The naive or simple one, here a young man utterly lacking judgment, 7:7, watched from a window as he walks unknowingly toward his own ruin. His folly is not stupidity but a failure to see danger clearly, exactly what wisdom's instruction exists to correct.

basic.context: This long passage completes the sustained warning against adultery begun in chapter 5. It opens with tender, almost domestic language, bind my teaching to your heart like a lamp for your path, then turns severe, comparing adultery to embracing fire, and finally becomes a short story: a father, watching from his window, narrates in painful detail how a naive young man is lured, seduced, and led like an animal to slaughter by a bold, deceptive woman.
basic.hermeneutics: The shift from direct command, 6:20 to 7:5, to narrated scene, 7:6 to 23, is a deliberate literary strategy. By showing rather than merely telling, the passage lets the reader watch temptation unfold in real time, twilight, a chance encounter, flattering words, an appeal to false piety, until the reader feels the same mounting momentum the young man does, and then meets the same abrupt, fatal outcome. The warning is not against womanhood or sexuality but against a specific pattern, seductive deception meeting an unguarded heart.
basic.originalLanguages: The nokriyah, adulteress, is literally 'the foreign one,' a woman made a stranger to her own marriage covenant through unfaithfulness. The husband's qinah, jealousy, in 6:34 names a righteous, unappeasable anger no bribe can satisfy, showing adultery is treated as a real wound to real people, not a private matter without cost. And the young man is a peti, one lacking judgment, 7:7, not stupid but unguarded, exactly the condition wisdom's teaching exists to correct.
basic.typology: The young man led 'like an ox going to the slaughter,' 7:22, uses the same image later applied to the Suffering Servant, who was 'led like a lamb to the slaughter,' Isaiah 53:7, a jarring contrast between a fool destroyed by his own folly and the innocent Christ who willingly bore a death He did not deserve for the very folly this passage describes.
basic.christ: This passage exposes how easily an unguarded heart is led toward destruction, following its own desires 'like an ox going to the slaughter.' The gospel takes up that very image and reverses it: Christ, wholly innocent, was 'led like a lamb to the slaughter,' Isaiah 53:7, not because He was deceived or unguarded but because He willingly bore the judgment that the folly and unfaithfulness this passage describes truly deserve. Where the young man's path led to Sheol, Christ entered death itself and rose, opening a road back to life for all who had wandered.
basic.god: God cares intensely about marital faithfulness, treating adultery's cost as real and severe, wounds, dishonor, and an unappeasable jealousy, not a private matter with no wider consequence. Yet He is also the source of the very instruction, likened to a lamp and a light, 6:23, that guards against this destruction, showing His concern to protect, not merely to condemn.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53:7 pictures the Suffering Servant led like a lamb to the slaughter, a deliberate contrast to the fool of 7:22. Matthew 5:28 extends the seventh commandment to the heart's desire, echoing 6:25. Hebrews 13:4 upholds the honor of marriage and the certainty of God's judgment on the unfaithful. James 1:14 to 15 traces the same trajectory from desire to sin to death.
basic.oneStory: This passage's vivid warning against a heart unguarded by wisdom, ending in a road to death, belongs to Scripture's larger story of humanity's wandering desires and the ruin they bring. That story finds its rescue in Christ, who was led to the slaughter not for His own folly but for ours, so that the road to Sheol this passage describes might be closed and a road back to life opened for all who turn to Him.

context.literary:
Read as one unit, 6:20 to 7:27 is built around two parental appeals that match each other. Each opens with the language of commandment and teaching, 6:20 and 7:1, each reaches for the same body pictures of binding words on the neck, the fingers and the tablet of the heart, 6:21 and 7:3, and each states its purpose in the same words: to keep you from the evil woman, 6:24, and from the adulteress, 7:5. Between them lies an argument, 6:25 to 35, and after them a story, 7:6 to 23. The argument works by two rhetorical questions about fire and hot coals, verses 27 and 28, then by comparison with a thief, verses 30 and 31, and ends in a verdict, verses 32 to 35. The story is the longest narrative in the book, and the father tells it as an eyewitness, looking down through the lattice of his window.

The scene has its own shape. Verses 6 to 9 set the stage, street, corner, twilight. Verses 10 to 13 bring the woman out to meet him. Verses 14 to 20 give her speech, seven verses long and the longest piece of direct speech in the passage. Verses 21 to 23 narrate the surrender. The young man never says a word. Every verb of motion is his, crossing, strolling, following, while the woman does all the talking and all the planning. The father then closes by widening the audience, from 'my son' in 6:20 and 7:1 to 'my sons' in 7:24, and by naming the house the whole story has been walking toward, 'her house' in 7:27.

The passage also sits where the book turns. It ends the father's long run of lectures in chapters 1 to 7, and Wisdom's own public speeches in chapters 8 and 9 answer it. The woman who 'lurks at every corner,' 7:12, is the dark counterpart of Wisdom who takes her stand at the crossroads, 8:2. Her invitation to a bed is met by Wisdom's invitation to a feast.
context.historical:
The first hearers lived in walled towns where the street, the square and the gate were the public rooms of life, and where houses had windows with lattices from which a householder could watch without being seen. The teacher's vantage point in 7:6 is an ordinary one. The woman is out at twilight, a time when the husband's absence and the dark would hide a meeting, and the text says plainly that her feet 'do not remain at home,' 7:11. Elsewhere the good wife is the one who 'watches over the affairs of her household,' Proverbs 31:27, so her wandering is a mark of the covenant she has left.

The law was clear. The seventh commandment forbids adultery, Exodus 20:14, and the Torah sets the penalty for both parties, Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22. Other ancient law collections also treated adultery as a grave offence against the husband. Proverbs speaks from the husband's side in 6:34 and 35, where a wronged man's rage cannot be bought off, and from the community's side in 6:33, where the shame sticks. The teacher is not drafting a legal code. He is showing a young man what the act costs in the world he actually inhabits.

Her speech is full of the vocabulary of worship and trade. A peace offering was a shared meal, and the flesh of a thanksgiving offering had to be eaten on the day it was offered, Leviticus 7:15, while a vow offering could be eaten that day or the next, Leviticus 7:16. So she has meat in the house and a pious reason to say so. The linen from Egypt and the myrrh, aloes and cinnamon of 7:16 and 17 are imported luxuries, and the same perfumes fill the garden of the lover in Song of Songs 4:13 and 14. She dresses an adulterous bed in the scents that Israel's poetry reserved for the marriage bed. Her husband carries 'a bag of money' on a long journey, a merchant on the roads, which tells the listener that she is not a woman in want.
context.canonical:
The passage draws on Deuteronomy before it speaks. The command to bind the words 'on your hands' and teach them 'when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up,' Deuteronomy 6:7 and 8, lies behind 6:21 and 22 and 7:3. The father takes Israel's confession of faith and applies it to one temptation. The 'apple of the eye' in 7:2 is the phrase Moses uses of how God guarded Jacob, Deuteronomy 32:10, so the teaching is to be guarded the way God guards His people.

The rest of the Old Testament supplies the cases the warning has in view. Joseph runs from his master's wife and leaves his cloak in her hand, Genesis 39:12. David strolls on his roof one evening and sees Bathsheba, 2 Samuel 11:2 to 4, and the cost, as the proverb says, falls on his house. Job swears that he has not lurked at a neighbour's door, because adultery 'is a fire that burns down to Abaddon,' Job 31:9 to 12, which reads like a commentary on 6:27 to 29. Ecclesiastes 7:26 calls the woman who is a snare 'more bitter than death.' The prophets then turn the picture round and make faithless Israel the adulterous wife, Jeremiah 3:20, Ezekiel 16:32 and Hosea 3:1.

The New Testament keeps both lines. Jesus moves the seventh commandment into the eye and the heart, Matthew 5:27 and 28, which is where 6:25 had already put it. Paul tells the Corinthians to flee sexual immorality because their bodies are members of Christ, 1 Corinthians 6:15 to 20. James traces desire, sin and death in one line, James 1:14 and 15, as the young man's walk does. Hebrews pairs honoured marriage with God's judgment, Hebrews 13:4, and Revelation sets the great prostitute against the bride, Revelation 17:1 to 5 against Revelation 19:7 and 21:2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The teacher wanted a young man to see himself in the story before he ever met the woman. That is why he chooses a scene instead of a rule. The youth is not wicked and not stupid; he is 'among the simple,' 7:7, someone on an ordinary evening walk who has never decided in advance where he will not go. Every step in the story is small, a different street, a slower pace, a glance at a corner, and the narrator marks each one so that the listener learns to recognise drift while it is still only drift.

He also wants the hearer to understand why the woman succeeds. She offers religion, a meal, privacy, flattery and certainty that no one will find out. None of it is true: the husband will return, the vow was no cover for sin, and the God who sees is not on a journey. The teaching about the hidden eye of the LORD in 5:21 is the unspoken answer to her 'my husband is not at home.'

And he wants the hearer to take the prescribed defence seriously. The remedy is not willpower in the moment. It is a relationship formed long before, a love for wisdom as close as a sister's, 7:4, and the words of the parents written on the heart, 7:3, so that when the voice at the corner speaks, the heart already has an answer. The warmth of the opening verses and the horror of the ending belong together, since the father is describing a rescue that has to begin at home.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The story in 7:6 to 23 is narrated, not commanded. The woman's speech is recorded because it is typical of seduction, not because her words are to be copied or her methods studied as a guide. The prescriptions in the passage are the direct ones: keep the teaching, 6:20 and 7:1, do not lust in the heart, 6:25, do not let the heart turn aside to her ways, 7:25. Everything in between is there to give those commands force.

Three cautions help in applying it today. First, the proverbs in 6:26 and 7:26 speak in sweeping terms of what the woman 'preys upon' and how many she has 'slain,' and these are warnings in vivid rhetoric, not statistics. Second, the passage addresses a son, and the same warning applies to a daughter and to wives, since the Bible's wider teaching on marital faithfulness binds husbands and wives alike. Third, the husband's unappeasable rage in 6:34 and 35 is a description of what jealousy typically does, not a command to take vengeance. The New Testament sends believers to the cross and not to the sword, and offers repentance and forgiveness where the proverb sees only ruin.

debates.question: Is the woman a literal adulteress, or a figure for Folly and idolatry?

views.label: A literal woman
views.case: The scene is full of concrete detail, a street, a husband away on business, a bed with Egyptian linen, and the law of Israel treats adultery as a real offence. The sages of Israel, writing for young men heading into public life, had good reason to teach about a plain danger. The proverbs about adultery elsewhere, such as Job 31:9 to 12 and Ecclesiastes 7:26, are also plainly literal.

views.label: A figure for Folly and false worship
views.case: The same vocabulary of the stranger and the smooth tongue is turned in chapter 9 on the woman Folly, who calls from her door in the same words, 9:13 to 18. The prophets use adultery as their standing picture for Israel going after other gods, Hosea 3:1 and Ezekiel 16:32. On this reading the youth is any simple person drawn off from covenant loyalty by a rival lover.

views.label: Both together
views.case: The teacher puts a real woman before the hearer and lets her stand for every voice that offers pleasure without the covenant. Chapter 9 then makes the link explicit by giving her a name, Folly, while keeping her marks, loud, seductive and deadly.

debates.bearing: The literal reading is the safest starting point, because the commands in 6:25 and 7:25 are about a heart and a body, not about an idea. The wider reading explains why the passage sits where it does, at the doorway of the two houses of chapters 8 and 9, and why the New Testament can use the same shape against false teaching, as in Revelation 2:20 to 22.

debates.question: What does the thief comparison in 6:30 to 35 teach?

views.label: An argument from the lesser to the greater
views.case: A starving thief is not despised and still must pay back sevenfold, so an adulterer, who has no hunger to plead, will pay far more. The point is that adultery has no excuse, and its cost cannot be settled by a payment.

views.label: A contrast of kinds of wrong
views.case: Theft can be repaid in goods, but no payment can restore a husband's honour. Verse 35 says he will take no ransom at all, so the proverb marks the line between a debt that money settles and a wound that it cannot.

views.label: A picture of the law's lesser penalty
views.case: Some point out that the Torah's prescribed penalty for adultery is death, Leviticus 20:10, while the proverb speaks only of scars and shame. On this view the sage is describing what a young man will meet in daily life, however the courts handle it.

debates.bearing: All three agree on the main thing: the harm cannot be bought back. That is why the passage is more than a social warning. It prepares the reader to see that some debts need a ransom beyond what the offender can pay, which the New Testament answers in Mark 10:45.

study.originalLanguages:
The woman is called 'the evil woman' and 'the adulteress,' 6:24, but in 7:5 she is also nokriyah, 'the stranger,' and the BSB footnote at 6:24 notes that the phrase can also be read 'the stranger.' The word means foreign, outside the family, and Proverbs 2:16 to 19 shows how it works: she is a woman who has abandoned the partner of her youth and forgotten the covenant of her God. What makes her a stranger is not her birthplace but her break with the covenant, and that is why a young man can meet her in his own street.

The young man is a peti, 7:7, from the root patah, 'to be open, to be enticed.' The same root appears in Exodus 22:16 where a man 'seduces' a virgin. A peti is someone whose mind is open to whatever comes in. The text then calls him chaser lev, 'lacking in heart,' which the BSB renders 'lacking judgment,' and the same phrase turns up in 6:32 for the adulterer himself and in 9:4 and 9:16 for the simple who are invited to two tables. In Hebrew thought the 'heart' is the seat of thought and decision, so to lack heart is to lack the faculty of weighing.

Verse 9 gives a quiet link back to the opening of the chapter. The BSB's 'dark of the night' is literally the 'pupil' of the night, ishon layla, using the same word as the 'apple of your eye' in 7:2, where the footnote also says 'literally the pupil.' The teaching is to be guarded like the pupil of the eye, and the young man goes out into the pupil of the night, the darkest part. One word frames a choice between guarding light and walking in dark.

In 6:34 jealousy is qinah, from the same root as the word for God's own jealousy for His people in Exodus 20:5. The BSB reads 'jealousy enrages a husband,' and the Hebrew is closer to 'jealousy is the heat of a man.' In 6:35 the 'ransom' is kofer, the word for the price paid to redeem a life. A husband will not accept it, which is the exact reverse of what the Bible says of God's mercy, where a ransom is accepted.

The seducer's persuasion in 7:21 is lekach, the word for 'teaching' in other proverbs, such as Proverbs 4:2. Her seduction is a counterfeit of the father's instruction: she too has a lekach, and it is smoother. Finally the animal images of 7:22 and 23, ox, deer and bird, are three pictures of a creature that does not know what the trap is for. The BSB footnote at 7:22 warns that the Hebrew of the middle line is uncertain and the 'deer' reading is a probable emendation, so the weight of the picture rests on the ox and the bird, and on the closing line, 'not knowing it will cost him his life.'

typology.fulfillment: The father says his teaching is a lamp and a light, a way of seeing the path in the dark of the city streets. The psalmist says the same of God's word, Psalm 119:105, and Jesus gathers the image into Himself: 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness,' John 8:12. The correspondence is real, since the lamp of the law has now become a Person who walks beside the traveller. The type falls short because a lamp only shows the way, while Christ is both the way and the One who carries the traveller home, John 14:6.

typology.type: The words written on the tablet of the heart, 7:3
typology.fulfillment: The father urges his son to write the teaching on the tablet of his heart, a task the son has to do himself. Jeremiah promised a day when God would 'inscribe it on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:33, and Paul says the Corinthians are 'a letter from Christ,' written 'not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3. The escalation is that what a son was told to do for himself, the Spirit now does within believers. The type is incomplete because the father's command rests on effort, while the new covenant rests on God's gift.

typology.type: The ransom that no husband will accept, 6:35
typology.fulfillment: The offended husband will take no ransom, no lavish gift, and the adulterer has nothing to offer that could settle the account. The Bible's answer is not to soften the verdict but to supply the ransom from another hand. Jesus came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, and 'gave Himself as a ransom for all,' 1 Timothy 2:6. The pattern does not fit exactly: this is a contrast rather than a likeness, and the Bridegroom here is not the offended husband refusing payment but the One who pays the price for the unfaithful.

typology.type: The faithless wife and the faithful Bridegroom
typology.fulfillment: The prophets cast Israel as an adulterous wife, Jeremiah 3:20 and Ezekiel 16:32, and Hosea is told to love his wife again 'though she is loved by another,' Hosea 3:1, as the LORD loves Israel. The proverb's adulteress is the same figure in the street. In Christ the Bridegroom, the story turns: He 'loved the church and gave Himself up for her' to present her 'holy and blameless,' Ephesians 5:25 to 27, and Paul fears the church may be led from 'a pure virgin' devotion to Him, 2 Corinthians 11:2. Revelation completes the contrast, with the great prostitute of 17:1 to 5 set against the bride of 21:2. The picture is of a whole people, not just of one man's fall.

study.christ:
This passage meets Christ at four points, and each one rests on texts the New Testament itself draws.

First, Christ is the one who keeps the heart that the father is trying to teach. The father asks a son to love wisdom as a sister, 7:4. Paul says Christ Jesus 'has become to us wisdom from God,' 1 Corinthians 1:30, and Hebrews says He 'is not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11. The invitation to treat wisdom as kin is answered in a surprising way: wisdom has taken our flesh and called us family, Hebrews 2:14. A young man who has lost his way is not told only to find a better principle but is offered a brother.

Second, Christ was tempted and did not fall. The young man is led by desire and drift, and James describes that line in James 1:14 and 15. Hebrews says Jesus 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. Because He has walked that road and kept His feet, He can sympathise with the simple and strengthen them, and the Spirit-given power to say no rests on His victory. This does not mean the Gospels record Him in a story like Proverbs 7. It means that the pressure the story describes was not foreign to Him.

Third, Christ answers the verse that has no answer in Proverbs. In 6:35 the wronged husband will accept no ransom. For the guilty reader that is a closed door. The gospel does not reopen it by lowering the standard but by providing the price: 'the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The cost the proverb says cannot be paid, Christ pays.

Fourth, Christ is the faithful Husband to an unfaithful people. The prophets treat adultery as the shape of Israel's sin, and Paul says believers were 'promised to one husband,' 2 Corinthians 11:2. Sexual sin in a believer is a wound to a union already made: 'your bodies are members of Christ,' 1 Corinthians 6:15. The ruin of Proverbs 7 is a road away from that union, and the call of Ephesians 5:25 to 27 is the road back.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The adulteress is not a type of any person in the Gospels, and the details of the bed and the road are not coded messages. The links above depend on the wider themes of covenant, wisdom, temptation and ransom that the New Testament itself brings to the passage.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who guards by teaching. The father presents the commandment as a lamp, 6:23, and the 'reproofs of discipline' as 'the way to life.' Instruction is not a fence built to spoil pleasure but a light set in the path of someone who cannot see in the dark. Behind every father's voice in Proverbs stands the God who speaks first, which is why the opening verses borrow Moses' words about binding His commands on hand and heart, Deuteronomy 6:6 to 9.

He sees what the couple think is hidden. Her argument depends on three things being true: her husband is away, it is dark and no one will know. Proverbs 5:21 has already said 'a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD,' and the passage shows the folly of building a plan on the absence of a watcher. The one who watches here is the father at the window, a small picture of the larger watching, and the God who sees is not on a journey with a bag of money.

He is a God of covenant faithfulness who takes faithfulness seriously. The prophets use adultery as the sharpest image for what betrayal of Him feels like, Hosea 3:1 and Jeremiah 3:20, and Malachi 2:14 says the LORD Himself is witness between a man and 'the wife of your youth.' That teaches something about God's own heart. He does not treat covenant breaking as a trifle, and His jealousy, Exodus 20:5, is not petty. It is love that refuses to be indifferent.

He is just and He is patient. The ruin in 7:23 to 27 is not a sudden bolt from heaven. It is the built-in end of a road, the consequence of what the young man chose, and the proverbs show that God's order carries its own warnings: fire burns, hot coals scorch, 6:27 and 28. Yet the warnings themselves are mercy. A God who wanted only to punish would not send a father to the window.

For worship, the passage invites two responses. One is to receive instruction as light rather than as limit, and to ask God to write His words on the heart, as He promised in Jeremiah 31:33. The other is gratitude that the same God who judges adultery also provides what 6:35 says no one can supply, the ransom, which He supplied in His Son. Reverence for a holy God and trust in a forgiving one belong together here.

crossReferences.note: Moses tells Israel to keep God's words on their hearts, teach them at home and on the road, tie them on the hands and write them on the doorposts. Proverbs 6:21 and 22 and 7:3 reuse that pattern. The father aims Israel's creed at a specific temptation, which shows how ordinary obedience and sexual faithfulness are joined.

The earlier lecture on the same theme sets 'water from your own cistern' against the stranger's embrace and ends by saying the wicked man's iniquities 'entrap him' and he dies for lack of discipline. Chapter 7 shows that same entrapment happening, so the two passages read as the argument and the illustration.

Joseph is grabbed by his master's wife and told 'Sleep with me!' He leaves his cloak in her hand and runs outside. It is the story-form of Proverbs 6:25 to 7:5: a man who has an answer ready and flees. It shows what the young man in chapter 7 needed and did not have.

One evening David walks on the roof and sees Bathsheba, and the fatal sequence of seeing, sending and taking follows. His fall is the case of a man far from simple, which shows the warning in 6:25 is not only for the naive. A king with every protection fell to the same drift.

Job swears he has not lurked at a neighbour's door, because adultery 'is a fire that burns down to Abaddon.' The image matches Proverbs 6:27 to 29 and calls the outcome by the name of the place of destruction, which is close to Sheol in 7:27. Two wisdom books reach for the same picture.

Folly is loud like the woman of 7:11, sits at the door of her house, and issues the same invitation as Wisdom word for word. The final line, her guests in the depths of Sheol, answers 7:27. Chapter 9 turns the young man's story into a general choice between two tables.

Jesus takes the commandment from the act to the look and the desire. Proverbs 6:25 had already said 'do not lust in your heart for her beauty.' Jesus does not add a new law but draws out what the wisdom teachers saw, that the path to the bed begins in the eye and the heart.

Paul answers the same sin with a new reason. A Christian's body is a member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit, and was 'bought at a price.' The command to flee in verse 18 resembles the father's 'do not stray into her paths,' but the motive is union with Christ rather than fear of consequences.

James describes temptation as being lured and enticed by one's own desire, which then conceives, bears sin, and grows into death. That is the story of Proverbs 7 in a sentence, from the first lure at the corner, to the act, to 'the chambers of death' at the end.

The Son of Man gives His life 'as a ransom for many.' In Proverbs 6:35 the husband will take no ransom, and the guilty have nothing to offer. Mark names the one ransom that is sufficient and freely given, which turns the closed door of the proverb into an open one.

John sees a woman with a golden cup, the 'great prostitute,' who makes the earth drunk on her immorality. She is Folly writ large, the adulteress as a world power. The chapter shows why Proverbs treats the seducer's house as a road to death: her cup is full of what looks sweet, as in Proverbs 9:17.

study.oneStory:
The story begins in Genesis, where the first temptation also arrives as a question about what is good to the eye, Genesis 3:6, and where the serpent's persuasion, like the woman's in Proverbs 7, gets its force from a promise that nothing will happen. 'You will not surely die,' Genesis 3:4, and 'my husband is not at home,' Proverbs 7:19, are two forms of one lie. The father at his window is doing what God did in the garden, speaking first, naming the danger and asking where the listener is going.

Israel then lived under a covenant that Scripture calls a marriage, with the LORD as husband and the people as bride, and the prophets read the nation's idolatry as adultery, Jeremiah 3:20, Ezekiel 16:32 and Hosea 3:1. Proverbs 7 is the same drama at ground level. The warning to a young man in a street is a small copy of the warning to a nation in a land. The ruin it describes, many 'slain,' 7:26, is what Israel's history shows on a large scale in exile.

Wisdom's reply comes in chapters 8 and 9, where she stands at the same crossroads and offers a feast instead of a bed. The story does not stop at the warning. It points to a Wisdom who is more than a poem. The New Testament says Christ has 'become to us wisdom from God,' 1 Corinthians 1:30, and the ransom the husband will not accept is paid by Him, Mark 10:45. The church, tempted by the world's cup, is called to remain a faithful bride, 2 Corinthians 11:2 and Ephesians 5:25 to 27.

The end of the story answers the road to Sheol with a different city. The 'great prostitute' of Revelation 17 is judged, her cup of abominations taken away, and the bride is revealed, 'prepared as a bride' for her husband, Revelation 21:2. There is no more seduction in that city because the Husband is present, and the people who once wandered at twilight are in a place where there is no night, Revelation 22:5. What the proverb teaches us to fear, a house whose chambers lead down to death, is finally replaced by the house where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3.

quiz.q: What are the father's teachings compared to in 6:22-23?

options.text: A lamp and a light that guide, guard, and speak throughout the day and night.
options.note: This is the exact image given, a lamp for walking, watching over sleep, and speaking upon waking.

options.text: A burden that restricts freedom.
options.note: The passage presents this teaching as protective guidance, not a restrictive burden.

options.text: A one time warning needed only once in youth.
options.note: The imagery of guiding by day and watching by night suggests continual, ongoing guidance, not a single early warning.

options.text: Advice useful only for financial decisions.
options.note: The immediate context applies this specifically to guarding against the adulteress, not finances.

quiz.q: How does 6:27-29 argue that adultery cannot be entered without cost?

options.text: By comparing it to embracing fire or walking on hot coals, both certain to burn.
options.note: Verses 27-28 use exactly this vivid double comparison.

options.text: By showing that some adulterers escape all consequences entirely.
options.note: The passage instead insists no one who touches another man's wife will go unpunished, verse 29.

options.text: By comparing it to a minor, easily healed injury.
options.note: The imagery of fire and hot coals suggests serious, not minor, harm.

options.text: By focusing only on financial loss.
options.note: Financial and social cost are named elsewhere, verses 31, 33, but this specific argument uses the fire and coals image for inevitable, serious harm generally, not finances alone.

quiz.q: In 7:14, what does the woman claim to have just done, and why is this significant?

options.text: She claims to have just offered peace offerings and paid her vows, using religious language and provision as a cover for seduction.
options.note: This detail shows how piety itself can be twisted into a mask for sin, a chilling feature of the scene.

options.text: She claims to be a foreigner with no local ties.
options.note: Her claim concerns sacrifices and vows, not her nationality.

options.text: She claims her husband has died.
options.note: She actually claims her husband is away on a journey, not deceased, verse 19.

options.text: She claims to be seeking legal advice.
options.note: Her stated purpose is explicitly seduction, dressed in religious language, not a legal matter.

quiz.q: What image describes the young man's fate in 7:22-23?

options.text: Like an ox going to the slaughter, not knowing it will cost him his life.
options.note: This is the passage's exact climactic image.

options.text: Like a shepherd leading his flock safely home.
options.note: This reverses the passage's actual image of being led toward destruction, not safety.

options.text: Like a soldier bravely facing a known danger.
options.note: The passage stresses his lack of awareness, not knowing, not deliberate bravery in the face of a known risk.

options.text: Like a merchant securing a profitable trade.
options.note: The passage's image is of unknowing destruction, not profit or gain of any kind.

quiz.q: How does the image of being 'led like an ox to the slaughter' relate to Christ?

options.text: It is reversed in Isaiah's picture of the innocent Servant led like a lamb to the slaughter, bearing judgment He did not deserve.
options.note: Isaiah 53:7 uses strikingly similar language for the Suffering Servant, in deliberate contrast to this fool's self caused ruin.

options.text: It shows that Christ was also guilty of folly like the young man in this passage.
options.note: Isaiah 53 explicitly presents the Servant as innocent, unlike the foolish young man here.

options.text: It has no connection to any New Testament image.
options.note: The slaughter imagery is picked up directly and significantly in Isaiah's Servant Songs, which the New Testament applies to Christ.

options.text: It only describes Old Testament sacrificial animals, with no further meaning.
options.note: This underplays the deliberate literary echo between a fool led to his own ruin and the innocent Servant led to bear others' ruin.

questions: The father describes his teaching as a lamp guiding both day and night. What ongoing, daily practice keeps God's word active as a guiding light in your life, rather than a lesson learned once and forgotten?

The woman in chapter 7 used religious language, having just paid her vows, as cover for seduction. Where might you be tempted to use spiritual language or activity to justify something you know is wrong?

The young man walked toward danger at twilight, in that vulnerable space between clear day and full dark. What are the twilight moments or situations in your own life where you are most vulnerable to temptation?
He followed her 'on impulse,' not realizing the cost until it was too late. What decision are you facing right now where you need to pause and count the cost before acting on impulse?

Christ was led like a lamb to the slaughter for sins He did not commit, so that those who wander toward ruin could be rescued. Where do you need to receive His rescue today, rather than trying to escape a snare on your own strength?

translationNotes.note: The levy of the prostitute renders a Hebrew phrase literally referring to the price paid for a loaf of bread, picturing prostitution's cost as reducing a man to poverty.
Apple of your eye renders a Hebrew idiom literally meaning the pupil, an image for something guarded with the utmost care and attentiveness.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and the rendering here follows the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Syriac; the Hebrew text as it stands reads more literally 'like fetters to discipline a fool.'

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Proverbs 6:20 through 7:27. Poetic line breaks in the source were rendered as flowing prose; the wording is otherwise unchanged and complete.
